A1-A2.headline: Discovering The Ancient Coastal Town Of Cherchell

pages.text: Walk along the quiet coast of Cherchell in Algeria today, and you step onto ancient ground. Sitting 89 kilometers west of Algiers, this seaside town once held different names and served as a busy port for old kingdoms.
pages.caption: The fountain place in Cherchell

pages.text:
In ancient times, people called this town Iol. Phoenician sailors built a trading post here around 600 BC. The oldest remains found at the site date from the fifth century BC.

Later, Carthage took control of the western coast. Iol became one of the most important trading posts in the region. By the third century BC, the town had strong walls and made its own bronze and silver coins. These early coins showed Punic writing and local fish.

Later, a king named Juba II took control of the area. In 25 BC, he renamed the city Caesarea to honor the Roman leader Augustus. Juba and his wife rebuilt the town with grand styles. They added a large theater, a lighthouse, and straight roads on a grid. Many people lived there peacefully.

The city grew very large and became a rich provincial capital. Roman soldiers and traders made the town very prosperous during this period.

Over time, the city faced many dangerous troubles and attacks. A Berber revolt damaged the town in 371. Later, invading groups called Vandals destroyed parts of the buildings.

Even after these heavy attacks, some ancient pieces survived. Today, visitors can see old walls, baths, and a theater that was later changed into an arena. Still, much of the old town is not fully known, and its ruins continue to teach us about life in North Africa.

B1-B2.headline: The Remarkable History Of Ancient Caesarea In Algeria

pages.text: Waves along Algeria's Mediterranean coast lap against Cherchell, a town 89 kilometers west of Algiers. Formerly known as Iol and Caesarea, this coastal settlement once served as a major capital for ancient kingdoms.
pages.caption: Fountain place in Cherchell town

pages.text:
Phoenicians established Iol around 600 BC, and the oldest remains found at the site date from the fifth century BC. By that time, Carthage had already taken control of Phoenician settlements in the western Mediterranean.

Punic Iol grew into an important trading post. In the third century BC, the fortified town minted Numidia's first bronze and silver coins, featuring Punic text and local fish.

In 25 BC, King Juba II received the city and renamed it Caesarea to honor Augustus. Juba and his Egyptian-born wife rebuilt the settlement on a grand scale, combining Roman and Hellenized styles.

The city flourished as a provincial capital under Roman rule, featuring a hippodrome, theater, temples, and rich suburban villas with mosaics. Its population likely reached up to 30,000 residents during the first two centuries.

Despite its prosperity, the city faced severe disruptions. A Berber revolt sacked the town in 371 and 372. Shortly after, Vandal raiders ravaged the area following their entry into North Africa.

Although battered by these conflicts, the city retained remarkable architectural monuments, including its famous theater and amphitheater, where early Christian martyrs like St. Marciana were supposedly killed during persecutions.

C1-C2.headline: Unveiling The Stratified Heritage Of Ancient Caesarea Mauretaniae

pages.text: Positioned on Algeria's Mediterranean littoral, Cherchell encapsulates millennia of Mediterranean history, evolving from a Punic entrepôt into a pivotal Roman provincial capital.
pages.caption: Historic fountain place in Cherchell

pages.text:
Initially established as Punic Iol around 600 BC, the settlement burgeoned into a sophisticated trading hub along the Algerian coast, though the oldest surviving remains date from the fifth century BC.

By the third century BC, fortified Iol was issuing Numidia's earliest bronze and silver coinage, bearing Punic inscriptions, Carthaginian deities, and motifs of local produce such as fish.

Following its annexation, King Juba II and Cleopatra Selene re-engineered the municipality, fusing Greco-Egyptian aesthetics with Roman urban planning, grid systems, and monumental architecture.

The ensuing pax Romana facilitated demographic expansion and opulence, culminating in an influential provincial capital boasting academies, fleets, and elaborate civic amenities.

Subsequent centuries introduced profound geopolitical instability. Destructive Berber insurrections in 371 and 372 preceded devastating Vandal incursions.

Furthermore, the municipal topography reflects complex architectural adaptations, such as the theater's conversion for hunting spectacles and the amphitheater where St. Marciana was supposedly martyred under Diocletianic persecution. These fragmentary remains underscore a deeply stratified archaeological record.
